title: Why so many jazz violinists came from Chicago
summary: Jones explains parents sent children to violin teachers and that church life was the main social circle.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Were there more jazz violin players in Chicago than anyplace else? I mean what -- Eddie South of course was more than just jazz. He played --
Gypsy. You know, more legitimate, really.

Yeah. But him, Ray Nance, Stuff, and then you talk about Ray having three violins in the front line. It sounds like there was a big concentration of jazz violinists. Moreso than any other city, wasn't there?
Well, coming up, when I was coming along, you either had a piano in your home or your parents would send you to a violin teacher.
It was the popularity of the instrument itself in the era.

Yeah. That was the thing to do at that time. You know, and you'd play in church. And the parents would like to show their children off, just like when I played the -- started playing some classical concerts, my piano teacher would give me -- Mr. Robinson, he would give concerts in the churches. That was our biggest social contact with everybody else, you know?
Well, life sort of revolved around what happened in the church.
Yes. So at -- that just happened to happen at that time. And I don't know. It was -- that was a good

question, because you know I never thought about that. Like when you were speaking about Ray Nance and the guys in his front line. His band was six pieces. But I forget who was in it. Something like John Kirby. Had they gotten out of Chicago and gotten to New York, they would have made it. Very unique, you know? Excuse me. But it just broke up and then pretty soon Ray wound up with Duke. And he evidently loved it, because he stayed there a long time, you know?
